recap.timezoneNote: All times shown in ET (America/New_York). Items marked headline were written only from the publisher's headline and summary. Today's closing-price, news and filings files were not available when this recap was written, so news coverage runs through about 10:00 PM ET on Nov 26, Friday's developments are not included, and story text does not quote closing moves.

driver.text: Per Bloomberg, AI uncertainty drove wild swings on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq ending down 0.6% after a sharp selloff (Nov 25, 4:17 PM ET); WSJ said the Nasdaq composite plunged as much as 4.5% before paring losses and that Treasury yields extended their fall after a flurry of U.S. data including the PCE price index. After the Thanksgiving break, Bloomberg reported Asian stocks rose for a second day along with US equity-index futures, extending a tentative recovery after weeks of volatility in the AI trade, while Treasuries declined as cash trading resumed (Nov 26, 4:59 PM ET); WSJ said Asian markets were mostly higher as sentiment around AI stabilized (9:13 PM ET), and Bloomberg reported China's industrial profits grew at the fastest pace in five months in October (9:18 PM ET). The Financial Times reported a hawkish Fed is poised to raise rates despite the stock market turmoil, with inflation the top concern for officials (Nov 26, 9:58 AM ET). In chips, WSJ reported Washington closed a loophole that let Chinese companies access Nvidia chips (Nov 26, 7:42 AM ET), and Bloomberg reported U.S. chip curbs are stalling AI data center financing across Asia (Nov 25, 9:49 PM ET). Written from headlines and publisher summaries only.

cryptoDriver.text: Per The Block, spot bitcoin ETFs have already hit record monthly net outflows of $5.39 billion in November, with several trading days remaining, putting them on track for their worst month on record. Written from the headline and the publisher's summary only.

items.headline: WSJ: U.S. officials say there's no evidence China coordinated Jensen Huang's affair
items.summary: WSJ reported that U.S. officials say there is no evidence China coordinated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair. Written from the headline and the publisher's summary only.

items.headline: WSJ: Nvidia's sales chief married an executive formerly at a company linked to chip smuggling
items.summary: Per WSJ, Nvidia's sales chief dated a Super Micro executive for years; they have now married, and her former company has been linked to chip smuggling. Written from the headline and the publisher's summary only.

items.headline: WSJ: Nvidia tells partners to pause shipments to Southeast Asia
items.summary: Per WSJ, Nvidia told partners to pause shipments to Southeast Asia; Washington recently closed a remote-access loophole that helped Chinese companies tap in to computing power in the region. Written from the headline and the publisher's summary only.
